newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel presents its 1997 budget to parliament.
newsitem.headline: Israel presents its 1997 budget to parliament.

text.p: Israel's Treasury Director-General David Brodett warned that the government could not afford to cut less than the planned 4.9 billion shekels as the 1997 budget was presented to parliament on Sunday.

"There is no substitute economic policy other than to accept budget cuts," said Brodett, who described the deficit target of 2.8 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) as "the absolute minimum for achieving economic targets".
But in contrast to recent remarks by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Brodett played down the prospect of further cuts. Netanyahu had said another one billion shekel cut might be needed.

The 190.8 billion shekel budget, which will be taken up for parliamentary debate on Tuesday and must be approved by December 31, has met opposition from parliament as well as cabinet members on grounds that the cuts fall hardest on the poor.

Brodett said the Treasury was basing 1997 spending on a 4.0 percent increase in GDP next year, a small improvement from this year's expected 3.8 percent growth but down sharply from the six to seven percent level in the 1990-95 period.

A key factor in the Treasury's ability to keep to revenue targets is the projected income from the sale of state enterprises. The 1997 budget projects privatisation revenues of 4.3 billion shekels, considerably more than has been achieved in recent years.
Budget Director Ron Croll told Reuters the figure was predicated on a new privatisation programme, which is expected to be released in November.

Officials expressed more concern about meeting revenue targets than controlling expenditures. "In the last two years we have not met deficit targets mainly because of revenue shortfalls," warned Tzippi Gal-Yam, head of state revenue administration.
Brodett would not commit himself to an exact estimate for the 1996 deficit. "If we're talking about the domestic deficit it will be something about four percent," he said.

A key goal of the fiscal restraint is to improve export profitability, which Brodett said was crucial to reviving economic growth. "The economic expansion of 1990-95 was led by the export sector," he said.

Improved export profitability would help the Treasury meet another target -- reducing a swelling current account deficit. The Treasury expects the deficit to reach 5.7 percent of GDP this year but fall to 4.5 percent in 1997.

The budget itself contains no significant changes from the one approved by the cabinet in July. The proposed cuts include reduced health-care subsidies, more stringent criteria for child allowances and lower defence spending.
The Treasury also proposes reducing investment subsidies to a ceiling of 20 percent from the current 34 percent.

Tax revenues are projected to grow 6.0 percent after inflation to 114.7 billion in 1997. The government expects to raise about 25 billion shekels in the domestic bond market, a 7.2 percent real increase from 1996.
